hypotheses.statement: Facebook use during the interval between two text messages predicts a decline in momentary affective well-being at the later time point, controlling for earlier affect.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: Specifically, we examined whether T2 affect (i.e., How do you feel right now? ) was predicted by T1-2 Facebook use (i.e., How much have you used Facebook since the last time we asked? ), controlling for T1 affect at level-1 of the model

hypotheses.statement: Average Facebook use over the 14-day period predicts a decline in life satisfaction (cognitive well-being) from pre to post, controlling for baseline life satisfaction and average emotion.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: we analyzed whether people's average Facebook use over the 14-day period predicted their life satisfaction at the end of the study, controlling for baseline life satisfaction and average emotion levels over the 14-day period

hypotheses.statement: Direct (face-to-face or phone) social interaction does not produce the same declines in affective and cognitive well-being that Facebook use does.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: An alternative explanation for these results is that any form of social interaction undermines wellbeing. Because we also asked people to indicate how frequently they interacted with other people ''directly'' since the last time we text messaged them, we were able to test this idea.

hypotheses.statement: The Facebook-use effect on well-being is not moderated by number of Facebook friends, perceived network support, depressive symptoms, loneliness, gender, self-esteem, time of participation, or motivation for using Facebook.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: They were also not moderated by the size of people's Facebook networks, their perceived supportiveness, motivation for using Facebook, gender, loneliness, self-esteem, or depression.

hypotheses.statement: Facebook use and direct social contact interact to predict changes in affective and cognitive well-being.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: Although we did not have a priori predictions about whether Facebook use and direct social contact would interact to predict changes in affective and cognitive wellbeing, we nevertheless explored this issue in our final set of analyses.

findings.notes: The sentence states 82 participants, but only one of the four race/ethnicity percentages (4.9%) is attainable as a share of 82. All four are simultaneously attainable at exactly one denominator in the searched range: 81. The most likely innocent explanation is straightforward and should be stated first -- one participant did not report race/ethnicity, so the percentages were computed over the 81 who did. The paper does not say so, and no missing-data note appears anywhere. A second candidate is that the recruited total was 81 and '82' is a slip. This rests on the paper's OWN stated n as the search ceiling, so the exclusion of n=82 is a fact about the paper rather than about a range I chose; but because a missing-response denominator fully explains it, this is recorded as suspicious and never as impossible. The tool itself returned 'consistent' because a joint denominator exists at all; the finding recorded here is the narrower and different fact that the stated denominator is not that joint one.

consequence.explanation: Sample-composition reporting only; no inferential claim in the paper depends on the race/ethnicity breakdown.

findings.notes: Rulebook rule 2 asks whether a thresholded p conceals an extreme value. It does not here, for a reason worth stating plainly: the paper PRINTS the chi-square statistic beside every thresholded p, so nothing is hidden -- the exact p is recoverable by any reader, as this check just did. An eleven-order-of-magnitude gap is simply what a chi-square of 65 on 4,589 observations produces, and style rules require reporting it as a floor. The same reasoning covers the other seven thresholded p-values in the paper. Correct reporting, not a finding.

findings.notes: FAMILY DEFINITION IS DOING A LOT OF WORK HERE AND THE CAVEAT MUST TRAVEL WITH THE NUMBER. The family I supplied is broad -- every significance test in the Results -- and under it both results significant at exact p (.02 and .02, the two life-satisfaction models) fall below every correction threshold. But those two are not independent claims: they are the SAME cognitive well-being outcome fitted with and without a loneliness covariate, so counting them as two is already generous. Under the narrower and quite defensible family of two primary outcomes, Bonferroni alpha is .025 and the cognitive result at p=.02 survives. The affective result is untouched under any reading: at chi-square 28.90 its true p is around 8e-08, orders of magnitude below any threshold. The honest statement is that the paper's FIRST headline claim is robust to multiplicity and its SECOND is fragile to it, and that the paper applies and mentions no correction anywhere. One further, unquantifiable factor: at least twelve moderation tests and two interaction tests are reported only as 'ps > .16' and 'ps > .44', and two more sit in the supplements, so the true comparison count exceeds the fifteen counted here. This is a FLOOR on the multiplicity problem.

consequence.explanation: Under the broad family, the abstract's second claim -- that the more people used Facebook over two weeks, the more their life satisfaction declined (t(73) = -2.39, p = .02) -- does not survive Bonferroni, Holm, Benjamini-Hochberg or Benjamini-Yekutieli correction; under a two-outcome family it does.

findings.notes: Two distinct problems in one place. FIRST, a broken cross-reference: the sentence directs the reader to Text S3 for the OLS regression coefficients, and Text S3 contains no regression output at all -- it is a single sentence about data availability. The models behind the paper's life-satisfaction claim (which predictors, entered how, with what standard errors and R-squared) are therefore documented NOWHERE, in the article or in any of the six supplements. SECOND, the sentence that is there is a textbook state-but-withhold declaration under rulebook rule 7: 'available upon request' is not availability. Neither observation involves any calculation. An innocent explanation for the first is a late renumbering of the six supplementary files -- but I read all six, and none contains the regression output, so the material appears never to have been supplied.

findings.notes: Text S6 is cited at the point where roughly twelve moderation tests are summarised, and it contains one sentence explaining why ONE motivation item was not tested. Not a single moderation coefficient, standard error, test statistic or exact p-value appears in the article or in any of the six supplements, all of which I read. The abstract nonetheless states these effects 'were also not moderated by' seven named variables. That is a null claim resting on an unreported minimum p-value. Recorded as a reporting finding, not an arithmetic one; no tool applies and none is missing. The innocent explanation -- that PLOS ONE in 2013 did not require exhaustive null reporting -- is real and should be stated, but it does not restore a reader's ability to check the claim.

findings.quote: They were also not moderated by the size of people's Facebook networks, their perceived supportiveness, motivation for using Facebook, gender, loneliness, self-esteem, or depression.

computed.method: absence_of_evidence was the appropriate check and could NOT be run: it requires either a confidence interval or a coefficient with its standard error, and the paper prints neither for any moderation test. Recorded as a refusal rather than a substituted calculation. Deriving a standard error myself from b and t would have been unguarded arithmetic and was not done.

findings.reproduction: no command applies -- absence-of-evidence requires an interval or a b/se pair, and the paper prints neither for any moderation test; this finding is a reading of the reporting, not an arithmetic result
findings.notes: 'Not significant' is not 'no effect'. With an analytic n around 77 and between-person moderators, the study has low power to detect moderation, so a minimum p of .16 is entirely compatible with moderating effects large enough to matter. Because no interval is printed, the largest moderating effect still consistent with these data cannot be computed -- by me or by any reader. The abstract states the null as a positive finding, which is the strongest form the claim can take and the one least supported by what is reported. A reporting-practice finding with no arithmetic in it, so nothing is missing from the toolkit here.

consequence.explanation: One of the four sentences in the abstract's results summary asserts an absence of moderation that the published statistics cannot bound.

findings.quote: ''direct'' social interaction did not predict changes in cognitive well-being, B = 2 .006, b = 2 .059, t (73) = 1.04, p =.30

computed.method: Sign comparison across the three statistics printed on one line; no arithmetic. In this PDF's text layer the minus sign renders as the digit 2, and it is present before .006 and .059 but absent before 1.04. The parallel sentence on the preceding page prints the sign consistently: 'B = 2 .012, b = 2 .124, t (73) = 2 2.39'.

findings.reproduction: no command applies -- this is a notation and sign reading of one printed line, not an arithmetic result
findings.notes: A t statistic carries the sign of the coefficient it tests. Both coefficients on this line are negative and the t is printed positive. Almost certainly a typesetting or transcription slip rather than anything substantive: the p-value is .30 either way, and I verified separately that |t| = 1.04 at df = 73 reproduces p = .30 exactly. Recorded only because the sentence supports an abstract-level claim, so the passage is load-bearing. One provenance caution: this PDF's font encoding renders minus as '2' throughout, which is why the neighbouring '2 2.39' reads oddly -- but the asymmetry between the two lines is in the source, not introduced by extraction.

consequence.explanation: The sign of the t does not change the p-value or the null conclusion drawn from it.

findings.reproduction: no command applies -- this is a comparison of printed coefficients across two models, not an arithmetic result
findings.notes: Two standardized coefficients of near-equal magnitude are reported with markedly different t statistics, in models fitted to the same participants. There is a completely ordinary explanation and it is probably the right one: the second model adds an apparently uncentred Facebook-use x direct-contact product term, and the resulting collinearity inflates the standard error of every term involving it, which is exactly how a sizeable beta ends up with a small t. I record this as INDETERMINATE rather than as a flag because I cannot distinguish that from a transcription error in the beta without the standard errors -- and the standard errors are precisely what Text S3 was cited to provide and does not. Deriving them myself from b and t would be unguarded arithmetic and I have not done it. This is where the missing supplement has its most concrete cost.

computed.method: A reading of what the paper does and does not print. The participant-level analytic n is never stated; the only trace of it is the residual df chain, which steps down by exactly one as each additional covariate is added (73 with 3 predictors, 72 with 4, 71 with 5) -- an internally coherent pattern. No sample size was computed from it here.

findings.reproduction: no command applies -- this records a value the paper never prints, not an arithmetic result
findings.notes: The paper reports the observation count (4,589) but never the participant count entering the OLS life-satisfaction models; a reader must infer it from the degrees of freedom. The df chain is at least self-consistent, stepping down by one per added covariate exactly as it should, which is a point in the paper's favour -- and I used that chain as my working n elsewhere in this sweep, labelling it an inference every time. Recorded as indeterminate because the figure is genuinely absent rather than wrong. It matters because Table 1's correlations, the twelve moderation tests and all three OLS models depend on an n the reader is never told.

findings.notes: No a-priori power analysis and no sample-size justification appear anywhere. This is unremarkable for a 2013 experience-sampling paper and is NOT offered as a criticism of the authors' conduct; it is recorded because it bears directly on the moderation nulls above. The participant-level tests run on roughly 77 people and the paper itself describes its effects as 'small', so the twelve null moderation tests are where an unstated power assumption does the most work.

figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Facebook use predicts declines in affect and life satisfaction over time. Interacting with Facebook during one time period (Time1-2) leads people to feel worse later on during the same day (T2) controlling for how they felt initially (T1); values are regression weights from multilevel analyses (Panel A). Average Facebook use over the course of the 14-day experience-sampling period predicts decreases in life satisfaction over time; values are standardized regression weights from OLS regression analysis (Panel B). * p , .05, ** p , .01, *** p , .001.

panels.shows: Path diagram of the lagged multilevel model: T1-2 Facebook use predicting T2 affect while controlling for T1 affect, annotated with regression weights and significance stars.
Path diagram of the OLS model: mean Facebook use over the 14 days predicting post life satisfaction controlling for pre life satisfaction, annotated with standardized regression weights.

unchecked.reason: Both panels are path diagrams annotated with regression weights. The two weights named in the caption's prose (the multilevel B and the standardized OLS beta) also appear in the Results text and were verified there, but the diagrams very likely also print the AUTOREGRESSIVE paths (T1 affect to T2 affect; pre to post life satisfaction) and possibly their significance stars, and those coefficients appear nowhere in the text or in Table 1. I did not run figure extraction, so any value carried only by the figure is unchecked. This is a specific, locatable gap in this review rather than a generic caveat.

The table states NO sample size, for either the within-person or the between-person half, and no n for it appears anywhere in the paper. Significance is shown only as asterisk thresholds, with no exact p-values. Only the single borderline cell (r = .22*) was close enough to .05 to be testable at all, and it was tested at the df-implied n of 77 with a consistent result. Every other cell is either far from a threshold or would require an n the paper does not supply.

unchecked.location: Results, Moderation -- roughly twelve moderator tests summarised as 'ps > .16'
unchecked.reason: No coefficient, standard error, test statistic, exact p or confidence interval is reported for any individual moderation test, in the article or in any of the six supplements. Text S6, cited at exactly this point, contains no moderation results. Nothing can be recomputed and no interval can be bounded.

unchecked.location: Results, Alternative explanations -- worry and loneliness interactions summarised as 'ps > .44'
unchecked.reason: Reported only as a minimum p across two interaction tests, with no statistics attached to either.

unchecked.location: Statcheck was deliberately NOT run over the body text
unchecked.reason: This PDF's font encoding renders every minus sign as the digit 2 and every chi-square as 'x2', so 't(73) = -2.39' appears in the text layer as 't (73) = 2 2.39'. Feeding that to statcheck would have it parse mangled statistics and report inconsistencies that are artifacts of extraction rather than properties of the paper. Instead I read each of the 17 test statistics against both the docling body text and the per-page text, and verified every one individually with recalc_stat_to_p. Coverage of the NHST statistics is therefore complete; only the automated scanner was skipped, and deliberately.

unchecked.location: Compliance arithmetic: 83.6% mean response rate, range 18.6%-100%, and 4,589 total observations
unchecked.reason: These can only be reconciled by choosing a denominator the paper does not state -- whether the 83.6% mean was taken over 79 completers or all 82 recruited, and whether the maximum per participant was 70 signals. No summation or proportion check applies without inventing that denominator, so none was run.

unchecked.location: SD plausibility for the five experience-sampled slider items (e.g. affect M=37.47, SD=25.88 on a 0-100 scale)
unchecked.reason: check_sd_range is CLI-only and not callable from this stage. In any case all five SDs sit far below the range/2 ceiling of 50 that the stated 0-100 bounds impose, so no violation is possible and the check would add nothing.

Not applicable and deliberately not run. The paper contains exactly one table and it is a correlation matrix, not a table of means and SDs. There is no second block of summary statistics to compare it against, within the paper or across studies.

Deliberately not run. The paper's effects are small (standardized beta = -.124 for the life-satisfaction outcome), which is entirely typical for social-psychological field data, and the authors themselves flag the effects as 'small' in their Caveats section. There is no implausibly LARGE effect for this check to adjudicate.

unchecked.location: GRIM on the SWLS, Social Provision Scale and UCLA Loneliness means
unchecked.reason: All three are means of multi-item composites, so their granularity is 1/(k*n) rather than 1/n. At roughly 80 participants and 5 or more items the attainable steps are finer than the second decimal place, so GRIM has no discriminating power and would return 'consistent' for essentially any printed value. Running it would manufacture false reassurance rather than evidence.
